claim: The rapid expansion of human activities threatens ocean-wide biodiversity.
source: The rapid expansion of human activities threatens ocean-wide biodiversity.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets the context for the study.

claim: Numerous marine animal populations have declined.
source: Numerous marine animal populations have declined, yet it remains unclear whether these trends are symptomatic of a chronic accumulation of global marine extinction risk.
evidence: This statement is supported by the broader scientific literature on marine biodiversity trends.

claim: One-quarter of chondrichthyan species are threatened according to IUCN Red List criteria due to overfishing.
source: We estimate that one-quarter are threatened according to IUCN Red List criteria due to overfishing (targeted and incidental).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the systematic IUCN Red List assessment conducted in this study.

claim: Large-bodied, shallow-water chondrichthyan species are at greatest risk.
source: Large-bodied, shallow-water species are at greatest risk and five out of the seven most threatened families are rays.
evidence: This finding is derived from the statistical analysis of life history and ecological correlates of threat status presented in the manuscript.

claim: Five out of the seven most threatened chondrichthyan families are rays.
source: Large-bodied, shallow-water species are at greatest risk and five out of the seven most threatened families are rays.
evidence: This is supported by the family-level threat analysis presented in Figure 6 and related text.

claim: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates.
source: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates, and only one-third of species are considered safe.
evidence: This comparison is based on the IUCN Red List assessments of different vertebrate groups as discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Only one-third of chondrichthyan species are considered safe.
source: Overall chondrichthyan extinction risk is substantially higher than for most other vertebrates, and only one-third of species are considered safe.
evidence: This is derived from the Red List assessment results showing the proportion of Least Concern species.

claim: Population depletion of chondrichthyans has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters.
source: Population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters, but is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis of threat distribution presented in the manuscript.

claim: Population depletion of chondrichthyans is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
source: Population depletion has occurred throughout the world's ice-free waters, but is particularly prevalent in the Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle and Mediterranean Sea.
evidence: This is supported by the geographic hotspot analysis shown in Figures 7-9.

claim: Human impacts over the past 10 millennia have profoundly and permanently altered biodiversity on land, especially of vertebrates.
source: There is increasing evidence that human impacts over the past 10 millennia have profoundly and permanently altered biodiversity on land, especially of vertebrates (Schipper et al., 2008; Hoffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on terrestrial biodiversity change.

claim: There is mounting concern for the increasing human influence on marine biodiversity that has occurred over the past 500 years.
source: The oceans encompass some of the earth's largest habitats and longest evolutionary history, and there is mounting concern for the increasing human influence on marine biodiversity that has occurred over the past 500 years (Jackson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jackson (2010) discussing historical marine biodiversity changes.

claim: The rapid expansion of fisheries and globalized trade are emerging as the principal drivers of coastal and ocean threat.
source: Notwithstanding the limitations of these biased snapshots, the rapid expansion of fisheries and globalized trade are emerging as the principal drivers of coastal and ocean threat (Polidoro et al., 2008; Anderson et al., 2011b; McClenachan et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on marine threats.

claim: The status of a few of the best-studied exploited fish species and ecosystems may be improving.
source: Recent insights from ecosystem models and fisheries stock assessments of mainly data-rich northern hemisphere seas, suggest that the status of a few of the best-studied exploited species and ecosystems may be improving (Worm et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Worm et al. (2009) regarding fisheries status.

claim: The improving status view is based on only 295 populations of 147 fish species and is far from representative of the majority of the world's fisheries and fished species.
source: However, this view is based on only 295 populations of 147 fish species and hence is far from representative of the majority of the world's fisheries and fished species, especially in the tropics for which there are few data and often less management (Sadovy, 2005; Newton et al., 2007; Branch et al., 2011; Costello et al., 2012; Ricard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous work, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Overfishing and habitat degradation have profoundly altered populations of marine animals.
source: Overfishing and habitat degradation have profoundly altered populations of marine animals (Hutchings, 2000; Lotze et al., 2006; Polidoro et al., 2012), especially sharks and rays (Stevens et al., 2000; Simpfendorfer et al., 2002; Dudley and Simpfendorfer, 2006; Ferretti et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on marine population changes.

claim: Overfishing and habitat degradation have especially altered populations of sharks and rays.
source: Overfishing and habitat degradation have profoundly altered populations of marine animals (Hutchings, 2000; Lotze et al., 2006; Polidoro et al., 2012), especially sharks and rays (Stevens et al., 2000; Simpfendorfer et al., 2002; Dudley and Simpfendorfer, 2006; Ferretti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations specifically focused on sharks and rays.

claim: Chondrichthyans arose at least 420 million years ago.
source: Chondrichthyans make up one of the oldest and most ecologically diverse vertebrate lineages: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs (Compagno, 1990; Kriwet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary history supported by citations.

claim: Chondrichthyans rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs.
source: Chondrichthyans make up one of the oldest and most ecologically diverse vertebrate lineages: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs (Compagno, 1990; Kriwet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to evolutionary and ecological studies.

claim: Chondrichthyans play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function.
source: Today, this group is one of the most speciose lineages of predators on earth that play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function (Ferretti et al., 2010; Heithaus et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ecological studies on the role of sharks and rays.

claim: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates.
source: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates, exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom (Cortés, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cortés (2000) on chondrichthyan life history.

claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom.
source: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates, exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom (Cortés, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cortés (2000).

claim: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival.
source: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival, rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality (Musick, 1999b; Cortés, 2002; García et al., 2008; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to life history and population dynamics studies.

claim: Chondrichthyans are intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality.
source: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival, rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality (Musick, 1999b; Cortés, 2002; García et al., 2008; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on chondrichthyan vulnerability to fishing.

claim: Chondrichthyans are often caught as incidental but retained as valuable bycatch of fisheries targeting more productive teleost fish species.
source: Chondrichthyans are often caught as incidental, but are often retained as valuable bycatch of fisheries that focus on more productive teleost fish species, such as tunas or groundfishes (Stevens et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stevens et al. (2005) on chondrichthyan fisheries.

claim: Fishing pressure on chondrichthyans is increasing as teleost target species become less accessible due to depletion or management restrictions.
source: In many cases, fishing pressure on chondrichthyans is increasing as teleost target species become less accessible (due to depletion or management restrictions) and because of the high, and in some cases rising, value of their meat, fins, livers, and/or gill rakers (Fowler et al., 2002; Clarke et al., 2006; Lack and Sant, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fisheries trends and chondrichthyan exploitation.

claim: Fins have become one of the most valuable seafood commodities.
source: Fins, in particular, have become one of the most valuable seafood commodities: it is estimated that the fins of between 26 and 73 million individuals, worth US$400-550 million, are traded each year (Clarke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clarke et al. (2007) on the shark fin trade.

claim: The fins of between 26 and 73 million chondrichthyan individuals, worth US$400-550 million, are traded each year.
source: Fins, in particular, have become one of the most valuable seafood commodities: it is estimated that the fins of between 26 and 73 million individuals, worth US$400-550 million, are traded each year (Clarke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Clarke et al. (2007) providing trade estimates.

claim: The landings of sharks and rays reported to FAO increased steadily to a peak in 2003 and have declined by 20% since.
source: The landings of sharks and rays, reported to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), increased steadily to a peak in 2003 and have declined by 20% since (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of FAO fisheries data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: True total chondrichthyan catch is likely to be 3–4 times greater than reported to FAO.
source: True total catch, however, is likely to be 3–4 times greater than reported (Clarke et al., 2006; Worm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on underreporting in fisheries.

claim: Most chondrichthyan catches are unregulated and often misidentified, unrecorded, aggregated, or discarded at sea.
source: Most chondrichthyan catches are unregulated and often misidentified, unrecorded, aggregated, or discarded at sea, resulting in a lack of species-specific landings information (Barker and Schluessel, 2005; Clarke et al., 2006; Iglésias et al., 2010; Bornatowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on fisheries data quality.

claim: Reported chondrichthyan catch has been increasingly dominated by rays, which have made up greater than half of reported taxonomically-differentiated landings for the past four decades.
source: The reported chondrichthyan catch has been increasingly dominated by rays, which have made up greater than half of reported taxonomically-differentiated landings for the past four decades (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of FAO data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Chondrichthyan landings were worth US$1 billion at the peak catch in 2003.
source: Chondrichthyan landings were worth US$1 billion at the peak catch in 2003, since then the value has dropped to US$800 million as catch has declined (Musick and Musick, 2011).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Musick and Musick (2011) on fisheries economics.

claim: The value of chondrichthyan landings has dropped to US$800 million as catch has declined since 2003.
source: Chondrichthyan landings were worth US$1 billion at the peak catch in 2003, since then the value has dropped to US$800 million as catch has declined (Musick and Musick, 2011).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Musick and Musick (2011).

claim: A main driver of shark fishing is the globalized trade to meet Asian demand for shark fin soup.
source: A main driver of shark fishing is the globalized trade to meet Asian demand for shark fin soup, a traditional and usually expensive Chinese dish.
evidence: This is a statement about the economic drivers of shark fishing.

claim: The trade in fins remains largely unregulated across the 86 countries and territories that exported >9,500 mt of fins to Hong Kong in 2010.
source: This particularly lucrative trade in fins (not only from sharks, but also of shark-like rays such as wedgefishes and sawfishes) remains largely unregulated across the 86 countries and territories that exported >9,500 mt of fins to Hong Kong (a major fin trade hub) in 2010 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of Hong Kong trade data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Of the 1,041 assessed chondrichthyan species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened.
source: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary result from the IUCN Red List assessment presented in Table 1.

claim: 25 chondrichthyan species (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered.
source: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU) (Table 1).
evidence: This is from the Red List assessment results in Table 1.

claim: 43 chondrichthyan species (4.1%) are assessed as Endangered.
source: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU) (Table 1).
evidence: This is from the Red List assessment results in Table 1.

claim: 113 chondrichthyan species (10.9%) are assessed as Vulnerable.
source: Of the 1,041 assessed species, 181 (17.4%) are classified as threatened: 25 (2.4%) are assessed as Critically Endangered (CR), 43 (4.1%) Endangered (EN), and 113 (10.9%) Vulnerable (VU) (Table 1).
evidence: This is from the Red List assessment results in Table 1.

claim: 132 chondrichthyan species (12.7%) are categorized as Near Threatened.
source: A further 132 species (12.7%) are categorized as Near Threatened (NT).
evidence: This is from the Red List assessment results.

claim: Chondrichthyans have the lowest percentage (23.2%) of Least Concern species of all vertebrate groups.
source: Chondrichthyans have the lowest percentage (23.2%, n = 241 species) of Least Concern (LC) species of all vertebrate groups, including the marine taxa assessed to date (Hoffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the Red List results and a citation to Hoffmann et al. (2010).

claim: Almost half (46.8%, n = 487) of chondrichthyan species are Data Deficient.
source: Almost half (46.8%, n = 487) are Data Deficient (DD) meaning that information is insufficient to assess their status (Table 1).
evidence: This is from the Red List assessment results in Table 1.

claim: At least a further 68 Data Deficient species are likely to be threatened.
source: Of the 487 DD species for which we had sufficient maximum body size (n = 396) and geographic distribution data (n = 378), we were able to predict that at least a further 68 DD species are likely to be threatened (Table 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on predictive modeling presented in Table 3.

claim: At least one-quarter (n = 249; 24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened.
source: Accounting for the uncertainty in threat levels due to the number of DD species, we estimate that more than half face some elevated risk: at least one-quarter (n = 249; 24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened and well over one-quarter are Near Threatened (Table 1).
evidence: This is an estimate that accounts for Data Deficient species, based on predictive modeling.

claim: Only 37% of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be Least Concern.
source: Only 37% are predicted to be Least Concern (Table 1).
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling that accounts for Data Deficient species.

claim: Most threatened chondrichthyan species are found in depths of less than 200 m.
source: Most threatened chondrichthyan species are found in depths of less than 200 m, especially in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and the Western Central Pacific Ocean (79.6%, n = 144 of 181, Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of depth distributions presented in Figure 2.

claim: 79.6% (n = 144 of 181) of threatened chondrichthyan species are found in depths of less than 200 m, especially in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and the Western Central Pacific Ocean.
source: Most threatened chondrichthyan species are found in depths of less than 200 m, especially in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and the Western Central Pacific Ocean (79.6%, n = 144 of 181, Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of depth distributions presented in Figure 2.

claim: Extinction risk is greater in larger-bodied chondrichthyan species found in shallower waters with narrower depth distributions.
source: Extinction risk is greater in larger-bodied species found in shallower waters with narrower depth distributions, after accounting for phylogenetic non-independence (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling presented in Figures 3 and 4 and Tables 3 and 4.

claim: The traits with the greatest relative importance (>0.95) for predicting threat are maximum body size, minimum depth, and depth range.
source: The traits with the greatest relative importance (>0.95) are maximum body size, minimum depth, and depth range.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of trait importance presented in Figure 3.

claim: Geographic range has a much lower relative importance (0.79) for predicting threat compared to body size and depth traits.
source: In comparison, geographic range (measured as Extent of Occurrence) has a much lower relative importance (0.79, Figure 3), and in the predictive models it improved the variance explained by 2% and the prediction accuracy by 1% (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis presented in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: The probability that a chondrichthyan species is threatened increases by 1.2% for each 10 cm increase in maximum body length.
source: The probability that a species is threatened increases by 1.2% for each 10 cm increase in maximum body length, and decreases by 10.3% for each 50 m deepening in the minimum depth limit of species.
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results.

claim: The probability that a chondrichthyan species is threatened decreases by 10.3% for each 50 m deepening in the minimum depth limit of species.
source: The probability that a species is threatened increases by 1.2% for each 10 cm increase in maximum body length, and decreases by 10.3% for each 50 m deepening in the minimum depth limit of species.
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results.

claim: Species with narrower depth ranges have a 1.2% greater threat risk per 100 m narrowing of depth range, after accounting for maximum body size and minimum depth.
source: After accounting for maximum body size and minimum depth, species with narrower depth ranges have a 1.2% greater threat risk per 100 m narrowing of depth range.
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results.

claim: Geographic range of chondrichthyans varies over six orders of magnitude, between 354 km2 and 278 million km2.
source: Geographic range, measured as the Extent of Occurrence, varies over six orders of magnitude, between 354 km2 and 278 million km2 and is positively correlated with body size (Spearman's ρ = 0.58), and hence is only marginally positively related to extinction risk over and above the effect of body size.
evidence: This is based on analysis of geographic range data.

claim: Geographic range is positively correlated with body size (Spearman's ρ = 0.58) in chondrichthyans.
source: Geographic range, measured as the Extent of Occurrence, varies over six orders of magnitude, between 354 km2 and 278 million km2 and is positively correlated with body size (Spearman's ρ = 0.58), and hence is only marginally positively related to extinction risk over and above the effect of body size.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between range and body size.

claim: The threat risk increases by only 0.5% for each 1,000,000 km2 increase in geographic range, accounting for body size and depth effects.
source: Accounting for the body size and depth effects, the threat risk increases by only 0.5% for each 1,000,000 km2 increase in geographic range (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results in Table 4.

claim: The maximum variance explained by life history and geographic distribution models was 69%.
source: The maximum variance explained was 69% (Table 4) and the predictive models (without controlling for phylogeny) explained 30% of the variance and prediction accuracy was 77% (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: The predictive models explained 30% of the variance and prediction accuracy was 77%.
source: The maximum variance explained was 69% (Table 4) and the predictive models (without controlling for phylogeny) explained 30% of the variance and prediction accuracy was 77% (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results in Table 3.

claim: One-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) are threatened.
source: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
evidence: This is based on the habitat-specific threat analysis.

claim: Almost half of neritic and epipelagic chondrichthyan species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
source: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
evidence: This is based on the habitat-specific threat analysis.

claim: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic chondrichthyan species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened.
source: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the habitat-specific modeling presented in Figure 5.

claim: Similar-sized deepwater chondrichthyan species have approximately 12% risk of being threatened.
source: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the habitat-specific modeling presented in Figure 5.

claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than their shallow-water relatives due to their slow growth and lower productivity.
source: While deepwater chondrichthyans, due to their slow growth and lower productivity, are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than their shallow-water relatives (García et al., 2008; Simpfendorfer and Kyne, 2009) for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on deepwater species vulnerability.

claim: For a given body size, deepwater chondrichthyans are less threatened than shallow-water species largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries.
source: While deepwater chondrichthyans, due to their slow growth and lower productivity, are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than their shallow-water relatives (García et al., 2008; Simpfendorfer and Kyne, 2009) for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the analysis presented in Figure 5 and inference about fishing accessibility.

claim: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family.
source: As a result of their high exposure to coastal shallow-water fisheries and their large body size, sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the family-level threat analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Sawfishes are arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes.
source: As a result of their high exposure to coastal shallow-water fisheries and their large body size, sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the family-level threat analysis and comparative assessment.

claim: Other highly threatened chondrichthyan families include wedgefishes, sleeper rays, stingrays, guitarfishes, angel sharks and thresher sharks.
source: Other highly threatened families include predominantly coastal and continental shelf-dwelling rays (wedgefishes, sleeper rays, stingrays, and guitarfishes), as well as angel sharks and thresher sharks; five of the seven most threatened families are rays.
evidence: This is based on the family-level threat analysis.

claim: Least threatened chondrichthyan families are comprised of relatively small-bodied species occurring in mesopelagic and deepwater habitats.
source: Least threatened families are comprised of relatively small-bodied species occurring in mesopelagic and deepwater habitats (lanternsharks, catsharks, softnose skates, shortnose chimaeras, and kitefin sharks, Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the family-level threat analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Local chondrichthyan species richness is greatest in tropical coastal seas, particularly along the Atlantic and Western Pacific shelves.
source: Local species richness is greatest in tropical coastal seas, particularly along the Atlantic and Western Pacific shelves (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on the spatial analysis of species richness presented in Figure 7A.

claim: The greatest uncertainty in chondrichthyan status is centered on four areas: Caribbean Sea and Western Central Atlantic Ocean, Eastern Central Atlantic Ocean, Southwest Indian Ocean, and the China Seas.
source: The greatest uncertainty, where the number of DD species is highest, is centered on four areas: (1) Caribbean Sea and Western Central Atlantic Ocean, (2) Eastern Central Atlantic Ocean, (3) Southwest Indian Ocean, and (4) the China Seas (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on the spatial analysis of Data Deficient species presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The megadiverse China Seas face the triple jeopardy of high threat in shallow waters, high species richness, and a large number of threatened endemic species, combined with high risk due to high uncertainty in status.
source: The megadiverse China Seas face the triple jeopardy of high threat in shallow waters (Figure 7CD), high species richness (Figure 7A), and a large number of threatened endemic species (Figure 8), combined with high risk due to high uncertainty in status (large number of DD species, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on the spatial analyses presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km2.
source: Indeed, the Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km2.
evidence: This is based on the spatial analysis of threat density.

claim: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic chondrichthyan species.
source: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic species (Figure 8; Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is based on the irreplaceability analysis presented in Figure 8.

claim: Over half of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (n = 561, 53.9%).
source: Over half of species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (n = 561, 53.9%, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on the predictive modeling that accounts for Data Deficient species.

claim: No chondrichthyan species has been driven to global extinction as far as we know.
source: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct (Dulvy et al., 2003; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of documented global extinctions, supported by citations.

claim: At least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct.
source: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct (Dulvy et al., 2003; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting local extinctions.

claim: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark (Carcharhinus hemiodon) is known only from 20 museum specimens captured in Southeast Asia and has not been seen since 1979.
source: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark (Carcharhinus hemiodon) is known only from 20 museum specimens that were captured in the heavily-fished inshore waters of Southeast Asia: it has not been seen since 1979 (Cavanagh et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cavanagh et al. (2003).

claim: The Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
source: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters (Cavanagh and Gibson, 2007; Gibson et al., 2008; Iglésias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on European chondrichthyan status.

claim: The Critically Endangered Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
source: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters (Cavanagh and Gibson, 2007; Gibson et al., 2008; Iglésias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on European chondrichthyan status.

claim: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa.
source: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa (Robillard and Séret, 2006; Harrison and Dulvy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on sawfish status.

claim: A very high percentage of chondrichthyan species are Data Deficient (46%, 487 species), which is one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon to date.
source: A very high percentage of species are DD (46%, 487 species); that is one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon to date (Hoffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with other taxa using data from Hoffmann et al. (2010).

claim: Maximum body size is an essential predictor of chondrichthyan threat status because of the close relationship between body size and the intrinsic rate of population increase in sharks and rays.
source: Maximum body size is an essential predictor of threat status, we presume because of the close relationship between body size and the intrinsic rate of population increase in sharks and rays (Smith et al., 1998; Frisk et al., 2001; Hutchings et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on life history and population dynamics.

claim: Depth-related geographic traits are more important for explaining chondrichthyan extinction risk than geographic range per se.
source: Our novel contribution is to show that depth-related geographic traits are more important for explaining risk than geographic range per se.
evidence: This is a key finding from the statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
source: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors (Figure 3). We hypothesize that this is so because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis and a hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Geographic range (measured as Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to chondrichthyan extinction risk.
source: We find that geographic range (measured as Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to extinction risk.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis showing weak relationship between range and risk.

claim: In terrestrial systems and the marine fossil record, small geographic range size is the principal correlate of extinction risk.
source: This is in marked contrast to extinction risk patterns on land (Jones et al., 2003; Cardillo et al., 2005; Anderson et al., 2011a) and in the marine fossil record (Harnik et al., 2012a, 2012b), where small geographic range size is the principal correlate of extinction risk.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on extinction risk in other systems.

claim: Fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans, and even species with the largest ranges are exposed and often entirely encompassed by the footprint of fishing activity.
source: We suggest that this is because fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans (Swartz et al., 2010), and even species with the largest ranges are exposed and often entirely encompassed by the footprint of fishing activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Swartz et al. (2010) and inference about fishing impacts.

claim: With a few exceptions (mainly eastern Atlantic slopes), fishing has a narrow depth penetration and hence species found at greater depths can still find refuge from exploitation.
source: By contrast, with a few exceptions (mainly eastern Atlantic slopes, Figure 7E), fishing has a narrow depth penetration and hence species found at greater depths can still find refuge from exploitation (Morato et al., 2006; Lam and Sadovy de Mitcheson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the spatial analysis in Figure 7E.

claim: The status of chondrichthyans is arguably among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage considered thus far, apart from amphibians.
source: The status of chondrichthyans is arguably among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage considered thus far, apart from amphibians (Stuart et al., 2004; Hoffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to assessments of other vertebrate groups.

claim: More than 30% of amphibians are threatened, but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
source: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
evidence: This is a comparison with amphibian Red List data.

claim: The high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with the emerging picture of the intense and unmanaged extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species.
source: Our discovery of the high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with the emerging picture of the intense and unmanaged extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species (Darwall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Darwall et al. (2011) on freshwater biodiversity threats.

claim: The chondrichthyan threat estimate is comparable to other marine biodiversity status assessments.
source: Our threat estimate is comparable to other marine biodiversity status assessments, but our findings caution that 'global' fisheries assessments may be underestimating risk.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about different assessment approaches.

claim: Of 1,568 IUCN-assessed Indo-Pacific coral reef ecosystem species, 16% (range: 12–34% among families) were threatened.
source: The only synoptic summary to-date focused on charismatic Indo-Pacific coral reef ecosystem species. Of the 1,568 IUCN-assessed marine vertebrates and invertebrates, 16% (range: 12–34% among families) were threatened (McClenachan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a citation to McClenachan et al. (2012).

claim: The 16% threat level for Indo-Pacific coral reef species is a conservative estimate because charismatic species are more likely to garner awareness and support for monitoring and conservation.
source: This is a conservative estimate of marine threat level because although they may be more intrinsically sensitive to extinction drivers, charismatic species are more likely to garner awareness of their status and support for monitoring and conservation (McClenachan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about bias in conservation assessments, supported by a citation.

claim: The predicted level of chondrichthyan threat (>24%) is distinctly greater than that provided by global fisheries risk assessments.
source: The predicted level of chondrichthyan threat (>24%) is distinctly greater than that provided by global fisheries risk assessments.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and other fisheries assessments.

claim: Global fisheries risk assessments provide modeled estimates of 18% collapsed stocks in data-poor unassessed fisheries and 7–13% in data-rich fisheries.
source: These studies provide modeled estimates of the percentage of collapsed bony fish (teleost) stocks in both data-poor unassessed fisheries (18%, Costello et al., 2012) and data-rich fisheries (7–13%, Branch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to fisheries assessment studies.

claim: Teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs.
source: This could be because teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs (Hutchings et al., 2012), but in addition we caution that analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries, particularly for species with less-resilient life histories.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hutchings et al. (2012).

claim: Analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries, particularly for species with less-resilient life histories.
source: This could be because teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs (Hutchings et al., 2012), but in addition we caution that analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries, particularly for species with less-resilient life histories.
evidence: This is a cautionary inference about potential biases in fisheries assessments.

claim: Quantitative analyses of Mediterranean data suggest five shark species had declined by 96% to >99.9% relative to their former abundance, meeting the Critically Endangered criteria.
source: Quantitative trends could be estimated for five species suggesting they had declined by 96% to >99.9% relative to their former abundance suggesting they would meet the highest IUCN Threat category of Critically Endangered (Ferretti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Ferretti et al. (2008) providing quantitative decline estimates.

claim: The median biomass relative to BMSY of 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
source: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
evidence: This is based on a citation to Costello et al. (2012) on fisheries status.

claim: The median biomass of shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
source: Assuming BMSY occurs at 0.3 to 0.5 of unexploited biomass then the median biomass of shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
evidence: This is an inference based on fisheries data from Costello et al. (2012).

claim: These biomass declines would be sufficient to qualify all of these 112 shark and ray fisheries for the Endangered IUCN category if they occurred within a three-generation time span.
source: These biomass declines would be sufficient to qualify all of these 112 shark and ray fisheries for the Endangered IUCN category if they occurred within a three-generation time span.
evidence: This is an inference about how fisheries declines relate to IUCN criteria.

claim: Empirical analyses show that an IUCN threatened category listing is triggered only once teleost fishes have been fished down to below BMSY.
source: Empirical analyses show that an IUCN threatened category listing is triggered only once teleost fishes (with far higher density-dependent compensation) have been fished down to below BMSY (Dulvy et al., 2005; Porszt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the relationship between IUCN criteria and fisheries reference points.

claim: The findings are consistent with only around one-quarter of chondrichthyan species having been fished down below the BMSY target reference point.
source: Hence, our findings are consistent with only around one-quarter of chondrichthyan species having been fished down below the BMSY target reference point.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of IUCN assessments with fisheries reference points.

claim: It is more likely that the conservative consensus-based approach has understated declines and risk in sharks and rays.
source: While there may be concern that expert assessments may overstate declines and threat, it is more likely that our conservative consensus-based approach has understated declines and risk in sharks and rays.
evidence: This is an inference about the direction of potential bias in the assessments.

claim: For marine species, predicting absolute risk of extinction remains highly uncertain because even with adequate evidence of severe decline, in many instances the absolute population size remains large.
source: For marine species, predicting absolute risk of extinction remains highly uncertain because, even with adequate evidence of severe decline, in many instances the absolute population size remains large (Mace, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mace (2004) on extinction risk assessment challenges.

claim: Red List categorization of chondrichthyans should be interpreted as a comparative measure of relative extinction risk.
source: Therefore, Red List categorization of chondrichthyans should be interpreted as a comparative measure of relative extinction risk, in recognition that unmanaged steep declines, even of large populations, may ultimately lead to ecosystem perturbations and eventually biological extinction.
evidence: This is a statement about how to interpret the Red List assessments.

claim: The Red List serves to raise red flags calling for conservation action, sooner rather than later, while there is still a chance of recovery and of forestalling permanent biodiversity loss.
source: The Red List serves to raise red flags calling for conservation action, sooner rather than later, while there is a still chance of recovery and of forestalling permanent biodiversity loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the purpose and utility of Red List assessments.

claim: There is still no global mechanism to ensure financing, implementation and enforcement of chondrichthyan fishery management plans that is likely to rebuild populations to levels where they would no longer be threatened.
source: Despite more than two decades of rising awareness of chondrichthyan population declines and collapses, there is still no global mechanism to ensure financing, implementation and enforcement of chondrichthyan fishery management plans that is likely to rebuild populations to levels where they would no longer be threatened (Lack and Sant, 2009; Techera and Klein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fisheries management gaps.

claim: One-quarter of threatened chondrichthyan species span the EEZs of 18 or more countries.
source: The proportion of species that are threatened increases markedly with geographic size measured by number of Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) spanned; one-quarter of threatened species span the EEZs of 18 or more countries (Figure 10).
evidence: This is based on analysis of species distributions across jurisdictions presented in Figure 10.

claim: Large geographic ranges of chondrichthyans do not confer safety, but instead exacerbate risk because they require coherent, effective international management.
source: Hence, their large geographic ranges do not confer safety, but instead exacerbates risk because sharks and rays require coherent, effective international management.
evidence: This is an inference about the management implications of wide-ranging species.

claim: With a few exceptions (e.g., Australia and USA), many governments still lack the resources, expertise, and political will necessary to effectively conserve the vast majority of sharks and rays.
source: With a few exceptions (e.g., Australia and USA), many governments still lack the resources, expertise, and political will necessary to effectively conserve the vast majority of shark and rays, and indeed many other exploited organisms (Veitch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Veitch et al. (2012) on conservation capacity.

claim: More than 50 sharks are included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention.
source: More than 50 sharks are included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention, implemented on the high seas under the 1992 Fish Stocks Agreement, but currently only a handful enjoy species-specific protections under the world's Regional Fishery Management Organizations (Table 6), and many of these have yet to be implemented domestically.
evidence: This is a statement about international legal frameworks for shark conservation.

claim: Currently only a handful of sharks enjoy species-specific protections under the world's Regional Fishery Management Organizations, and many of these have yet to be implemented domestically.
source: More than 50 sharks are included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention, implemented on the high seas under the 1992 Fish Stocks Agreement, but currently only a handful enjoy species-specific protections under the world's Regional Fishery Management Organizations (Table 6), and many of these have yet to be implemented domestically.
evidence: This is based on review of RFMO management measures presented in Table 6.

claim: The Migratory Sharks Memorandum of Understanding adopted by the Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species so far only covers seven sharks.
source: The Migratory Sharks Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) adopted by the Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) so far only covers seven sharks, yet there may be more than 150 chondrichthyans that regularly migrate across national boundaries (Fowler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fowler (2012) on migratory species.

claim: There may be more than 150 chondrichthyans that regularly migrate across national boundaries.
source: The Migratory Sharks Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) adopted by the Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) so far only covers seven sharks, yet there may be more than 150 chondrichthyans that regularly migrate across national boundaries (Fowler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fowler (2012).

claim: Only one of the United Nations Environment Programme's Regional Seas Conventions, the Barcelona Convention for the Conservation of the Mediterranean Sea, includes chondrichthyan fishes.
source: To date, only one of the United Nations Environment Programme's Regional Seas Conventions, the Barcelona Convention for the Conservation of the Mediterranean Sea, includes chondrichthyan fishes and only a few of its Parties have taken concrete domestic action to implement these listings.
evidence: This is a statement about regional conservation agreements.

claim: Only ten sharks and rays had been listed by CITES up to 2013.
source: Despite two decades of effort, only ten sharks and rays had been listed by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) up to 2013 (Vincent et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vincent et al. (2014) on CITES listings.

claim: A further seven species of shark and ray were listed by CITES in 2013.
source: A further seven species of shark and ray were listed by CITES in 2013—the next challenge is to ensure effective implementation of these trade regulations (Mundy-Taylor and Crook, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mundy-Taylor and Crook (2013).

claim: Many chondrichthyans qualify for listing under CITES, CMS, and various regional seas conventions.
source: Many chondrichthyans qualify for listing under CITES, CMS, and various regional seas conventions, and should be formally considered for such action as a complement to action by Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMOs) (Table 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the threat assessment results.

claim: Bans on 'finning' are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
source: Bans on 'finning' (slicing off a shark's fins and discarding the body at sea) are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
evidence: This is a statement about current conservation measures.

claim: Finning prohibitions have not significantly reduced shark mortality or risk to threatened species.
source: While these prohibitions, particularly those that require fins to remain attached through landing, can enhance monitoring and compliance, they have not significantly reduced shark mortality or risk to threatened species (Clarke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clarke et al. (2013) on the effectiveness of finning bans.

claim: The main threats to chondrichthyans are overexploitation through targeted fisheries and incidental catches (bycatch), followed by habitat loss, persecution, and climate change.
source: The main threats to chondrichthyans are overexploitation through targeted fisheries and incidental catches (bycatch), followed by habitat loss, persecution, and climate change.
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis conducted in the study.

claim: One-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing.
source: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: Some of the most threatened chondrichthyan species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
source: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: Shark-like rays, especially sawfishes, wedgefishes and guitarfishes, have some of the most valuable fins and are highly threatened.
source: Shark-like rays, especially sawfishes, wedgefishes and guitarfishes, have some of the most valuable fins and are highly threatened.
evidence: This is based on the threat and trade analysis.

claim: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37).
source: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37), while low-value fins often enter trade as well, even if meat demand is the main fishery driver (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of species in the fin trade.

claim: Nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181) are jeopardized by four principal processes of habitat degradation: residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, river engineering, and pollution.
source: In coastal, estuarine, and riverine habitats, four principal processes of habitat degradation (residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, river engineering, and pollution) jeopardize nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: Over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
source: The combined effects of overexploitation and habitat degradation are most acute in freshwater, where over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
evidence: This is based on the habitat-specific threat analysis.

claim: The degradation of coastal, estuarine and riverine habitats threatened 14% of sharks and rays.
source: Specifically, the degradation of coastal, estuarine and riverine habitats threatened 14% of sharks and rays: through residential and commercial development (22 species, including river sharks Glyphis spp.); mangrove destruction for shrimp farming in Southeast Asia (4 species, including Bleeker's variegated stingray Himantura undulata); dam construction and water control (8 species, including Mekong freshwater stingray Dasyatis laosensis), and pollution (20 species).
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: Population control of sharks due to their perceived risk to people, fishing gear, and other fisheries has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 species.
source: Population control of sharks, in particular due to their perceived risk to people, fishing gear, and other fisheries has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 species (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: The threatened status of only one chondrichthyan species has been directly linked to climate change (New Caledonia catshark Aulohalaelurus kanakorum).
source: So far the threatened status of only one species has been directly linked to climate change (New Caledonia catshark Aulohalaelurus kanakorum, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is based on the threat analysis.

claim: The climate-sensitivity of some sharks has been recognized.
source: the climate-sensitivity of some sharks has been recognized (Chin et al., 2010) and the status of shark and ray species will change rapidly in climate cul-de-sacs, such as the Mediterranean Sea (Lasram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on climate impacts on sharks.

claim: The status of shark and ray species will change rapidly in climate cul-de-sacs, such as the Mediterranean Sea.
source: the climate-sensitivity of some sharks has been recognized (Chin et al., 2010) and the status of shark and ray species will change rapidly in climate cul-de-sacs, such as the Mediterranean Sea (Lasram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lasram et al. (2010).

claim: Elevated extinction risk in sharks and rays is a function of exposure to fishing mortality coupled with their intrinsic life history and ecological sensitivity.
source: Elevated extinction risk in sharks and rays is a function of exposure to fishing mortality coupled with their intrinsic life history and ecological sensitivity (Figures 2–6).
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings from the statistical analyses.

claim: One-third of all chondrichthyan species have been described in the past thirty years.
source: One-third of all species have been described in the past thirty years.
evidence: This is a statement about the rate of taxonomic discovery.

claim: Scientists have described a new chondrichthyan species, on average, almost every 2–3 weeks since the 1970s.
source: Scientists have described a new chondrichthyan species, on average, almost every 2–3 weeks since the 1970s (Last, 2007; White and Last, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic reviews.

claim: Since 2005, scientists have recognized an additional ∼140 living chondrichthyan species.
source: Since Leonard V J Compagno completed the global checklist in 2005, scientists have recognized an additional ∼140 species (mostly new) living chondrichthyan species.
evidence: This is a statement about taxonomic progress since the baseline checklist.

claim: The increase in the rate of chondrichthyan descriptions in recent years is primarily associated with the lead up to the publication of a revised treatment of the entire chondrichthyan fauna of Australia.
source: This increase in the rate of chondrichthyan descriptions in recent years is primarily associated with the lead up to the publication of a revised treatment of the entire chondrichthyan fauna of Australia (Last and Stevens, 2009), requiring formal descriptions of previously undescribed taxa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Last and Stevens (2009).

claim: Three CSIRO special publications published in 2008 included descriptions of 70 previously undescribed chondrichthyan species worldwide.
source: In particular, three CSIRO special publications published in 2008 included descriptions of 70 previously undescribed species worldwide (Last et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2008c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the CSIRO publications.

claim: The number of new chondrichthyan species described in 2006, 2007 and 2008 was 21, 23, and 81, respectively.
source: The number of new species described in 2006, 2007 and 2008 was 21, 23, and 81, respectively, with all but nine occurring in the Indo–West Pacific.
evidence: This is a statement about the rate and geographic distribution of new species descriptions.

claim: Many more as yet undescribed chondrichthyan species exist.
source: Many more as yet undescribed chondrichthyan species exist.
evidence: This is a statement about expected future taxonomic discoveries.

claim: The chondrichthyan faunas in several parts of the world (e.g., the northern Indian Ocean) are poorly known.
source: The chondrichthyan faunas in several parts of the world (e.g., the northern Indian Ocean) are poorly known and a large number of species are likely to represent complexes of several distinct species that require taxonomic resolution, for example some dogfishes, skates, eagle rays, and stingrays (Iglésias et al., 2010; White and Last, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic reviews.

claim: A large number of chondrichthyan species are likely to represent complexes of several distinct species that require taxonomic resolution.
source: The chondrichthyan faunas in several parts of the world (e.g., the northern Indian Ocean) are poorly known and a large number of species are likely to represent complexes of several distinct species that require taxonomic resolution, for example some dogfishes, skates, eagle rays, and stingrays (Iglésias et al., 2010; White and Last, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic studies.

claim: Many areas of the Indian and Pacific Oceans are largely unexplored and it is likely that many more chondrichthyan species will be discovered in the future.
source: Many areas of the Indian and Pacific Oceans are largely unexplored and, given the level of micro-endemism documented for a number of chondrichthyan groups, it is likely that many more species will be discovered in the future (Last, 2007; Naylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on chondrichthyan diversity and biogeography.

claim: Recent surveys of Indonesian fish markets revealed more than 20 new shark species out of approximately 130 recorded in total.
source: For example, recent surveys of Indonesian fish markets revealed more than 20 new species of sharks out of the approximately 130 recorded in total (White et al., 2006; Last, 2007; Ward et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to surveys of Indonesian sharks.

claim: The IUCN Red List assessment involved 17 workshops with more than 300 experts.
source: We applied the Red List Categories and Criteria developed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) (IUCN, 2004) to 1,041 species at 17 workshops involving more than 300 experts who incorporated all available information on distribution, catch, abundance, population trends, habitat use, life histories, threats, and conservation measures.
evidence: This is a description of the assessment methodology.

claim: 302 national, regional, and international experts from 64 countries participated in the GSRLA workshops and the production of assessments.
source: In total, 302 national, regional, and international experts from 64 countries participated in the GSRLA workshops and the production of assessments.
evidence: This is a description of the expert participation in the assessment.

claim: Most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) were assessed using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.
source: We assessed most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.
evidence: This is a description of the assessment methodology.

claim: 29 threatened chondrichthyan species were assessed using the IUCN geographic range Criterion B.
source: The remaining threatened species were assessed using the IUCN geographic range Criterion B (n = 29) or the small population size and decline Criterion C (n = 4: Borneo shark Carcharhinus borneensis, Colclough's shark Brachaelurus colcloughi, Northern river shark Glyphis garricki, and Speartooth shark Glyphis glyphis).
evidence: This is a description of the assessment methodology.

claim: 4 threatened chondrichthyan species were assessed using the small population size and decline Criterion C: Borneo shark, Colclough's shark, Northern river shark, and Speartooth shark.
source: The remaining threatened species were assessed using the IUCN geographic range Criterion B (n = 29) or the small population size and decline Criterion C (n = 4: Borneo shark Carcharhinus borneensis, Colclough's shark Brachaelurus colcloughi, Northern river shark Glyphis garricki, and Speartooth shark Glyphis glyphis).
evidence: This is a description of the assessment methodology.
